issue_context.title: Migrate from github.com/docker/distribution to github.com/distribution/distribution/v3
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:
Kubernetes libraries have a dependency on `github.com/docker/distribution`
#### What you expected to happen:
Kubernetes libraries have a dependency on `github.com/distribution/distribution/v3`. Note the github org just changed, its the same project. I believe the v2 -> v3 was mostly to get around go.mod weirdness with versions, rather than large breaking changes, but am not sure.
#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Look at go.mod, I suppose

#### Anything else we need to know?:
`github.com/docker/distribution@v2.7.1+incompatible`, the library in use, is 2.5 years old. It does not have a go.mod file, and in turn depends on a bunch of other libraries without go.mod files. This generally makes importing these libraries a pain - you can see 350 projects needing to add `replace` hacks to go.mod to work around these issues: https://github.com/search?q=%22replace+github.com%2Fdocker%2Fdistribution%22&type=code

It would be great to upgrade to the latest version.

review_comments:
the `strings.ToLower(name[:i]) == name[:i])` bit is interesting and was added in https://github.com/distribution/distribution/pull/2979/files

does this mean an image spec of `Foo/bar` that previously was treated as `docker.io/Foo/bar` is now treated as `FOO/bar`? does dockerhub disallow mixed- or upper-case in repository names?

- Heh, yes, I ran exactly into this issue as well; https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/46378

This line is honestly quite hard to read due to the double-negatives everywhere (and I started to rewrite it, to make it easier to follow).

After some head-scratching, I _THINK_ it's correct, using the following reasoning;

> The test considered `Foo/bar` to be an invalid name, with the assumption that it was `[docker.io]/Foo/bar`. However, this was incorrect, and the test passed because the reference parsing had a bug; if the first element (`Foo`) is not lowercase (so not a valid namespace /  "path element"), then it *should* be considered a domain (as uppercase domain names are valid).

That said, the whole "maybe it's a domain" "maybe not" has always been somewhat fuzzy, and I suggested tagging the initial release as `v0.5.0` to still have some room before "v1.0.0".


/cc @milosgajdos @dmcgowan to verify if the new behavior is indeed _correct_ (and not an unexpected side-effect of fixing the other issue linked in that PR)

if dockerhub currently requires all namespaces to be lowercase, then this is fine, I just wanted to make sure no one was currently successfully using `Foo/bar` to refer to a `docker.io/Foo/bar` image in a way this would break

ha, we got a unit test failure as well:

```
{Failed;  === RUN   TestParseImageName
    parsers_test.go:52: ParseImageName(ROOT) expects error couldn't parse image name "ROOT": invalid reference format: repository name (library/ROOT) must be lowercase but did not get one
--- FAIL: TestParseImageName (0.00s)
```

looks like we were leaning on the underlying parser to reject this name and it no longer does

> if dockerhub currently requires all namespaces to be lowercase,

This is correct, Docker Hub does not allow mixed case, only lowercase, but it goes further than that, `docker` cli doesn't support uppercase repository names either. I am not familiar with other tools like `podman`, etc

```shell
$ docker tag hello-world Foo/bar
Error parsing reference: "Foo/bar" is not a valid repository/tag: invalid reference format: repository name must be lowercase
```

Thanks Milos! Yes, so it's definitely correct from that perspective; the only _possible_ change is that someone using `HELLO/world` would previously end up on `docker.io/HELLO/world` (and an error likely), and in the new situation, `HOST` would be considered a hostname, so potentially, a request can be made to `http(s)://HELLO/.....`

I don't expect huge issues with that, but it's worth mentioning.
